To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) high OC supply rates caused U(IV) to be mobilized in previously bioreduced sediments, and (2) low OC supply rates did not maintain the reducing condition of previously bioreduced sediment for a long time.
the supply rate of organic carbon (OC), the amount of OC, and the amount of residual Fe(III) all influence uranium (U) mobilization in previously bioreduced sediment.
the supply rate of OC to a bioreduced U-contaminated sediment has an impact on the mobility of U(IV) and that the OC supply rates need to be optimized to prevent the release of U(IV).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate of U(IV) and the role of OC in the remobilization of uranium in a previously U(IV)-bioreduced contaminated sediment.
understanding the fate of U in previously bioreduced U-contaminated sediments.
the mechanisms responsible for U mobilization and the factors that influence U mobilization in previously bioreduced sediments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a bioreduction strategy is not a long-term solution to the problem of U contamination in groundwater.
a low OC supply rate is not sufficient to maintain a reducing environment in U-contaminated sediments.
the bioreduction-based strategy is not a sustainable strategy for remediating U(IV) contaminated sediments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a low rate of OC supply can minimize U mobilization but cannot sustain the reducing condition for long times.
the OC supply rate is a critical factor to control the mobility of U(IV) under reducing conditions.
bioremediation is not a long-term solution for remediating U-contaminated sediments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is necessary to supply OC continuously for long time to maintain a reducing environment in the sediment, and to minimize the formation of U(VI).
it is necessary to maintain a reducing environment to prevent the remobilization of bioreduced U(II).
the bioreduction-based remediation strategy is not sustainable in a contaminated site where groundwater influx is high.
